verdict.bash.title.line1: You're burning tokens on a printf.
verdict.bash.title.line2: Cron plus a template and you're done.
verdict.bash.message: From your answers, this job is deterministic. Every agent run pays again for the system prompt, the tool definitions and the tool responses, and it ends with the same sentence every time. A script makes the call, fills the template and runs from cron without spending a token.
verdict.bash1call.descriptor: a script with one model call
verdict.bash1call.title.line1: Fixed pipeline, the model matters in one spot.
verdict.bash1call.title.line2: Call it there and nowhere else.
verdict.bash1call.message: Most of the flow is mechanical and judgement is needed in one step. Script the rest and call the model only there, with a short prompt and a constrained response format such as a JSON schema. You pay for one call per run instead of an agent looping through every step.
verdict.burn.title.line1: Messy input, unpredictable steps, judgement needed.
verdict.burn.title.line2: Go ahead and burn. Set a spending cap first.
verdict.burn.when: An agent is the right tool when the input is messy, the steps change from case to case and judgement is needed almost everywhere. From your answers, that's your case.
verdict.burn.message: A script would have to predict every branch and would stall at the first surprise. Use the agent, with a spending cap, a log of every run and a person checking the outputs that matter.
verdict.letItWrite.descriptor: have the agent write the script
verdict.letItWrite.title.line2: Have the agent write the script, review it, let it run.
verdict.letItWrite.message: The job repeats often enough that running an agent every time is wasted money. Use it once: ask it for the script, read it line by line, test it on a few real cases and ship it. You pay for tokens once, then the script runs without spending any.
